specAnchors.text: understand the nature of the following intermolecular forces: i London forces (instantaneous dipole-induced dipole) ii permanent dipole-permanent dipole interactions iii hydrogen bonds

primer.text: Between neighbouring molecules sit three ranks of attraction, none of them true covalent bonds. This note separates the bonds inside a molecule from the weaker pulls between molecules, then ranks the trio: fleeting induced dipoles, permanent dipoles, and the special case where hydrogen meets oxygen, nitrogen or fluorine. Master the ranking order now; it explains boiling points, solubility and melting behaviour later.

modules.title: Forces within and between molecules
modules.opening: Every molecule is held together inside by covalent bonds, yet a liquid or solid only coheres because of much weaker pulls acting across separate molecules. This lesson splits the two families apart, names the three intermolecular types, and sets the strength ladder that every later topic climbs.
keyPoints: Intramolecular forces operate inside one molecule and are ordinarily covalent bonds built from shared electron pairs.
Single, double, triple and co-ordinate bonds all count as intramolecular forces.
Intermolecular forces act between neighbouring molecules and are far weaker than the bonds inside them.
The three intermolecular types are induced dipole-dipole, permanent dipole-dipole, and hydrogen bonding.
A hydrogen bond reaches only about one tenth of a covalent bond's strength, which keeps the ladder honest.

low.restatement: Inside a molecule the shared pairs form strong covalent bonds; between molecules sit three weaker attractions that decide how easily the substance melts or boils.
low.analogy: Covalent bonds are the stitching that holds each shirt together, while intermolecular forces are the Velcro dots letting shirts stick to each other in the drawer.
low.examPointer: Never call an intermolecular attraction a bond when a question asks for force types - keep 'bond' for the covalent links inside the molecule and score the distinction mark.

medium.restatement: The electron pairs shared between nuclei give intramolecular covalent bonding; the between-molecule attractions are ranked induced dipole-dipole, then permanent dipole-dipole, with hydrogen bonding as a strengthened sub-case of the permanent type.
medium.analogy: Picture scaffolding poles welded into one frame (intramolecular) versus magnets letting separate frames cling together (intermolecular) - welding always wins the strength contest.
medium.examPointer: Compare strengths in the order asked: covalent bond, then hydrogen bond, then permanent dipole-dipole, then induced dipole-dipole - inversions cost the mark every session.

modules.title: Induced dipoles and their relative strength
modules.opening: Even molecules with no permanent polarity attract each other. This lesson follows the wandering electron cloud that creates momentary dipoles, shows how those moments induce partners in neighbours, and then ranks induced against permanent dipoles when molecule size is held equal.
keyPoints: Induced dipole-dipole forces exist between every pair of atoms or molecules, polar or not.
A shifting electron cloud can pile up on one side, making a temporary dipole that induces a matching dipole next door.
The attracted ends are the positive region of one molecule and the negative region of its neighbour.
Because the clouds never stop moving, the dipoles stay temporary and the forces stay weak.
At equal electron count, permanent dipoles outpull induced ones, so propanone boils higher than butane.

low.restatement: Electron clouds jitter constantly; an accidental lopsided cloud makes a momentary dipole whose positive end draws the negative side of a neighbour, and the cycle repeats everywhere.
low.analogy: Two shy commuters on a swaying bus: one leans accidentally toward the other, who then leans back - the sway keeps creating fresh pairs of lean-ins.
low.examPointer: Say 'temporary dipole induces a dipole in the neighbour' in that order when describing the mechanism - examiners award the sequence.

medium.restatement: Instantaneous asymmetry of the electron cloud gives a fleeting dipole; its electric field polarises the adjacent cloud, and the correlated flicker is the induced dipole-dipole attraction.
medium.analogy: A generator flickering on and off induces current in a nearby coil only while it runs - here the running never stops, so the induced pull persists statistically.
medium.examPointer: When asked to compare isomers or similar molecules, count electrons first: equal electron count means the induced contribution matches, so any boiling gap must come from the next force type up.

modules.title: Permanent dipoles and hydrogen bonding
modules.opening: Polarity that never switches off changes the game. This lesson follows the permanent dipole-dipole attraction between polar molecules, then meets hydrogen bonding: the supercharged case where hydrogen bonded to oxygen, nitrogen or fluorine reaches a neighbour's lone pair.
keyPoints: Polar molecules carry a permanent positive end and negative end because of bond polarity.
Permanent dipole-dipole forces attract the positive end of one molecule to the negative end of its neighbour.
Hydrogen bonding is the strongest intermolecular attraction and a special case of permanent dipole interaction.
It needs hydrogen covalently bonded to oxygen, nitrogen or fluorine, whose lone pair faces the exposed hydrogen.
Water's oxygen holds two lone pairs, so one water molecule can form two hydrogen bonds.

low.restatement: A molecule with an uneven charge map always attracts its neighbours end to end; when hydrogen sits on oxygen, nitrogen or fluorine, the pulled-apart hydrogen bonds to a lone pair nearby.
low.analogy: Bar magnets in a drawer never lose their poles, so they click together the same way every time; hydrogen bonded molecules are the strongest magnets in the set.
low.examPointer: Draw hydrogen bonds as dashed lines running from the lone pair to the delta-positive hydrogen - solid lines or missing ends lose the diagram mark.

medium.restatement: Bond polarity gives a fixed dipole whose ends align across molecules; attaching hydrogen to the most electronegative elements concentrates so much positive character at hydrogen that a lone pair from another molecule completes an unusually strong link.
medium.analogy: A permanently exposed Velcro strip (the delta-positive hydrogen) grabs the nearest loop (the lone pair) - ordinary dipoles only press fabrics together, they never hook.
medium.examPointer: Quote the donor condition exactly - hydrogen covalently bonded to O, N or F - and name the lone pair destination when sketching the link.

glossary.definition: A force acting inside a single molecule, in practice a covalent bond of any order holding its atoms together.
A far weaker attraction acting between neighbouring molecules, deciding melting and boiling behaviour.
The weakest intermolecular attraction, made when a flickering electron cloud creates a temporary dipole that polarises a neighbour.
The strongest intermolecular attraction, formed where hydrogen bonded to oxygen, nitrogen or fluorine reaches a lone pair on a neighbouring molecule.
